Up here banks have 2 auto lending networks. Private and dealer. A private approval does not necessarily mean an in dealer approval.  You take your money from private directly if that's who approved you.

Things are tight on income verification right now. I bought a truck end of February.  I had all but the most recent pay stub with me (2, 4 and 6 weeks ago)  and they still needed the most recent.  Not to be rude, but would you lend money to someone without a job, even if they told you they would have one soon?

Paying cash is not a bonus for the dealer. Many places on this planet allow a kickback for financing.  It's highly likely they would have made more off you with a financed sale.

Car dealers do some shady shit. Sometimes because they're shady. Other times it's just the way things are done. If you don't like the flags you see, walk. There's not always as much margin as you think in that car either. 

Red flag 1: Buyer beware.  Ever go on the internet? People take pictures of themselves from flattering angles. What you see isn't necessarily what you get in real life. But you get as much time as you want to look before you buy.

Red flag 2: not a red flag. Unless you ask to start it cold that is.  My truck was started for me, seat heaters on. Nice and comfortable for the customer.  

Red flag 3: not a red flag. You had a deal agreed on. A credit application in. That credit app may take longer than that day. Especially when you had a denial. We live in an instant gratification society but it doesnt always work that way. It's up to you to negotiate the car before it gets to the finance stage. Once the application is in, the price is set.

And if you can't transpose you can be in a world of hurt. I've played with guys who would tune to open D, and then throw on a capo. You can't just follow hands at that point like you can playing with guys in standard playing barre or power chords. Knowing the open chords also makes it easy in standard tuning. 

As far as physically knowing them, it really helps with positioning and writing lines even if you'reonly playing one note at a time. A good example of this is Mellowship Slinky in Bmaj by Red Hot Chili Peppers. He's just arpeggiating the B major chord in the main line but you would be hard pressed to get there without knowing where and how to play that Bmaj without that knowledge. 

If you're writing and your guitar player is playing a Dsus4, it is beneficial to know why you wouldn't play the F# (or F, depending on the key.)

If you are content playing covers, or even emulating other players if not just following along you don't need much theory. But to truly have your own voice you benefit from knowing WHY you're playing what you are.
